name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,670

clue.text: People in general will get half-cut here

indicators.note: cutting something in half keeps just one of its halves, here the opening part of the word

blocks.note: the public is people in general; only its first half survives

explanation.surface: Ordinary folk end up a bit drunk in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, which makes the surface work, but cryptically it says to keep half of PUBLIC. 'Here' is the definition, pointing at the place the clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A British bar is precisely the venue where drinkers become tipsy, so the whole clue describes the location named by 'here'.

clue.text: Tranquillity Base involved in step

indicators.note: something involved in another is wrapped up inside it

blocks.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
a pace is a single stride

explanation.surface: Tranquillity Base, the Apollo 11 landing site, wrapped up in Armstrong's famous small step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tranquillity Base' reads as one name, but it splits: 'Tranquillity' is the definition and 'Base' gives E, the mathematical constant.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm, quiet and freedom from disturbance are what both words describe, making them direct synonyms.

clue.text: Tabs freak chewed for sustenance in the morning?

indicators.note: food that is chewed gets mashed into a different shape, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone obsessed with tabs gnaws on them to get through the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tabs' can be slang for cigarettes or pills, which colours the surface; here the two words are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The first meal eaten after waking is the food that sustains a person through the early part of the day.

clue.text: Taken advantage of plonk and in good mood at work

blocks.note: to plonk something down is to put it
feeling up means cheerful
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Someone exploited at their job, cheered only by cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plonk' looks like the British word for cheap wine, but it is the verb meaning to set down heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exploited or imposed on by others is described by this adjective, meaning their good nature is abused.

clue.text: Bump into agent that's brought over more stout?

indicators.note: bringing something over turns it upside down, which in a down entry flips its order
one thing going into another ends up surrounded by it

blocks.note: a rep is a sales agent
a bump is a lump

explanation.surface: Running into a barman who has brought another pint of Guinness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' suggests the dark beer, fitting the pub scene, but here it is the adjective meaning fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout as an adjective means rounded and fat; the comparative of plump is a synonym for 'more stout'.

clue.text: Listener intruding on row is more obviously upset

indicators.note: an intruder pushes its way inside, so one piece goes into the middle of the other

blocks.note: a tier is a row of seats
the ear does the listening

explanation.surface: An eavesdropper butting in on an argument makes someone even more upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts as a quarrel, matching the upset, but it is a row of seats, a tier.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone closer to crying shows their distress more visibly, so being nearer to weeping means more evidently distressed.

clue.text: Pain in the arse stealing foremost of Tesco’s bread

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its very first letter
a thief takes the loot and holds it inside, so one piece ends up within another

blocks.note: PITA is the initialism for 'pain in the arse' (or ass)
the opening letter of the supermarket's name

explanation.surface: An annoying shoplifter pinches a loaf from Tesco, a big British supermarket chain.
explanation.walkthrough: PITA is internet shorthand for an irritating person; the extra T turns one spelling of the flatbread into the British one.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a flat, slightly leavened Middle Eastern loaf that opens into a pocket, so it is a type of bread.

clue.text: A right-hand man won't rub me the wrong way

indicators.note: doing something the wrong way means not in the proper order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A trusty assistant promises never to irritate the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'rub someone the wrong way' (annoy them) hides the anagram signal inside an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy or chief assistant is often called the second in command, the person ranked just below the leader.

clue.text: Gentleman getting European gold hat in Paris

blocks.note: a chap is a man
standard abbreviation
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A man wins Olympic gold for Europe and buys a hat while in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' signals that the answer is the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: This is simply the French word for a hat, the headwear one would ask for in a French shop.

clue.text: Conservative fit to become an old Lib-Dem leader

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
fit for a task means able

explanation.surface: A Tory deemed suitable to take over the Liberal Democrats.
explanation.walkthrough: Vince Cable led the Liberal Democrats, a UK centrist party, from 2017 to 2019, after serving in the coalition with the Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Vince Cable is a former party chief, so the surname identifies a past head of the Liberal Democrats.

clue.text: Where a hack might be employed on occasion?

definitions.text: Where a hack might be employed

blocks.clueFragment: Where a hack might be employed
blocks.note: first meaning: a hack is a journalist, who might work for The Times newspaper
second meaning: sometimes, now and then

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a tool or a computer intrusion; it is crossword slang for a journalist, placing them at a London daily.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means occasionally or now and then, while read literally it names a newspaper workplace.

clue.text: Do wrong hugging mostly embarrassed temptress

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter goes
to hug is to wrap arms around, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to sin is to do wrong
an embarrassed face goes red

explanation.surface: Misbehaving by embracing a blushing seductress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hugging' and 'temptress' paint a seduction, but the embrace is purely structural: a shortened colour sits inside the wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth the Sirens lured sailors to ruin, so the word now means any alluring, dangerous woman.

clue.text: Very gloomy-looking judge hoovering up line

indicators.note: a vacuum cleaner sucks things up inside itself, so one piece is swallowed by another

blocks.note: beak is British slang for a magistrate
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A grim magistrate snorting a line of cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoovering up line' hints at drug-taking; Hoover is the British word for vacuuming, and a beak is a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleak outlook or landscape is dreary and cheerless, so the adjective matches a gloomy appearance.

clue.text: A pervert I smacked around's one out for booty

indicators.note: something smacked around is knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A confession of beating up a creep who was chasing bottoms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booty' tempts as slang for buttocks, matching the pervert; it is plunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A privateer was a privately owned armed ship licensed to seize enemy vessels and keep the plunder, a legalised pirate.

clue.text: Plain-spoken French knight tucks into pastry

indicators.note: to tuck into a place is to slip inside it

blocks.note: an eclair is a cream-filled choux pastry
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A blunt French knight scoffing a cream cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucks into' looks like eating, but it says the knight slips into the pastry's letters, just after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means in plain language, uncoded, used of messages sent without encryption.

clue.text: Trick question Her Maj put to men and William?

blocks.note: a con is a trick
standard abbreviation
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
OR, other ranks, are the soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: The Queen poses a trick question to the troops and to Prince William.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William' suggests the modern prince next to the Queen, but the question mark points to William I, who took England in 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: William of Normandy is known by this epithet, so his title serves as a definition by example.

clue.text: Woke in English seaside resort after bishop’s left

indicators.note: something that has left has gone away, so its letter drops out

blocks.note: Brighton is a resort town on England's south coast
chess abbreviation for a bishop

explanation.surface: Someone waking up in a seaside town after the bishop has gone home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woke' reads as the past tense of wake, but it is the adjective for being alert to social injustice.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal adjectives for holding fashionably progressive, socially aware views, sometimes used mockingly.

clue.text: Bloomers really pleased one old girl no end

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: glad means pleased
the Roman numeral
standard abbreviation
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An elderly woman delighted endlessly by her new underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' are baggy old-fashioned knickers in the surface, but here they are things that bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: These tall garden plants produce spikes of showy flowers, so they are blossoming plants.

clue.text: Section of an outfit possibly indicating turret of a Panzer?

definitions.text: possibly indicating turret of a Panzer?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sleeveless pullover, one garment in a set of clothes

blocks.clueFragment: possibly indicating turret of a Panzer?
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: the upper part of an armoured vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outfit' also means a military unit, which ties the clothes to the German armoured vehicle; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The garment is a sleeveless knitted pullover, while the words taken literally describe the upper part of an armoured fighting vehicle.

clue.text: Coach with facial hair under nose earl sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending a letter up moves it higher, so it is lifted out and slotted back in nearer the top

blocks.note: tache is British slang for a moustache, the hair beneath the nose
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A trainer sporting a moustache, under the gaze of a snooty aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The E at the bottom of TACHE is the earl; it is moved up the column to sit after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: To coach someone is to train or instruct them, the same as giving lessons.

clue.text: I'm breathless taking in piece from Indian artist

indicators.note: a single piece taken from a word is one of its letters, here the first
to take something in is to absorb it inside

blocks.note: the speaker is gasping, so is one who pants
the word's opening letter

explanation.surface: A diner gasping after eating something from an Indian restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks in the first person: someone saying 'I'm breathless' is a panter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes pictures with brushes and pigment is a visual artist, one of the commonest examples.

clue.text: Go and nut ordinary couple of fellows

blocks.note: nut is slang for head
standard abbreviation
F is the abbreviation for fellow, so two of them

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and headbutt a pair of ordinary blokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is British slang for headbutting someone, which makes the surface violent; here it is simply the noun for a head.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off or depart is to leave, so the phrasal verb is an informal synonym for going.

clue.text: Houses full of British gentlemen on the Costas

indicators.note: something full of another holds it inside

blocks.note: homes are houses
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Villas packed with British expats on Spain's coasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Costas are the Spanish holiday coasts popular with Britons, so the answer is the Spanish word for men.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Spanish word for men, so it is what males would be called along Spain's coastline resorts.

clue.text: Shot provided that must be served up flaming?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: provided means if, as a condition
flaming red is the colour of fire

explanation.surface: A shot of liquor that has to be set alight before serving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' suggests a drink, which goes with flaming; it is the past tense of shoot.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun that was shot was discharged, so both past-tense verbs describe launching a bullet.

clue.text: Minimal working around one uni then another for Al

indicators.note: letters set to work are put into action in a new arrangement
one piece placed around others encloses them

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university
a second university

explanation.surface: A small job at one college, then another, all for a man named Al.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Al' looks like a man's name, but it is the chemical symbol; the rearranged letters wrap round the two Us.
explanation.definitionFit: Al is the chemical symbol for this light silvery metal, element 13, spelt the British way.

clue.text: Silly-billy I spot mainlining premier bit of ice

indicators.note: the premier or first bit of a word is its opening letter
mainlining puts a drug straight into a vein, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a spot is a dot
the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A fool admits to seeing someone injecting top-grade crystal meth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice' is slang for crystal meth, hence the drug picture; the first letter of it goes inside DOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly-billy is a foolish person, and the answer is the everyday word for someone stupid.

clue.text: Sure to get hot with Fahrenheit over record at front

indicators.note: the part at the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: hot, meaning fashionable, is in
standard abbreviation
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A weather report: certain to warm up, with the thermometer passing a new high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'above' but is the cricket term, abbreviated O; 'hot' means trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'in for' something, like a shock or a treat, means it is certain to happen to you.

clue.text: Shot of heroin the boss of Hoskins sorted out

blocks.note: an addict's dose is a fix
the setter Hoskins answers to the editor, ED

explanation.surface: The setter's boss gets him his drugs and so he's sorted.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so his boss is the crossword editor, abbreviated ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mended or resolved has been repaired or dealt with, so both mean the problem is settled.

clue.text: Musician goes on about one with touch of talent

indicators.note: going about something means encircling it
just a touch of a word is a tiny part, its first letter

blocks.note: someone who harps on goes on and on
the Roman numeral
the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A performer droning on about a person with a flicker of ability.
explanation.walkthrough: To harp on is to keep talking tediously about something, which supplies the instrument's verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of the large stringed instrument is a specific example of a person who makes music.

clue.text: Chilled American airport involved in grass

indicators.note: something involved in another is caught up inside it

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass
LAX is the code for Los Angeles International

explanation.surface: A laid-back American smuggling cannabis through an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' suggests cannabis, matching 'chilled', but it is a plant, the reed.
explanation.definitionFit: Chilled is informal slang for calm and laid-back, an easygoing state free from tension.

clue.text: Soldiers and performers will get shots after services

blocks.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a turn is an act on a variety bill

explanation.surface: Troops and entertainers having drinks after a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Services' suggests church or military ones, but it is tennis: the shot that answers a serve.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis the stroke that sends back an opponent's serve is called by this name, played straight after it.

clue.text: Blue movies BAFTA recognised at last!

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of each word

blocks.note: the closing letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A cheer that the British film academy has finally honoured porn films.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue movies' reads as one phrase for porn, but 'Blue' alone is the definition. BAFTA is Britain's film and TV awards body.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue is an idiom for being unhappy or low in spirits, so it means downcast.
